passages.title: Jeremiah receives his call
passages.summary: Jeremiah is a priest’s son from the village of Anathoth. The LORD’s word comes to him in the days of King Josiah. God says he knew Jeremiah before he was formed in the womb. He has appointed him a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah answers that he is only a youth and cannot speak. The LORD touches his mouth and puts words in it. Jeremiah sees an almond branch and a boiling pot tilted from the north. God promises to make him like a fortified city against the whole land.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me teaches that God knew Jeremiah before birth. How does God answer Jeremiah’s fear about speaking?

contextNote.title: The call sets the book's two directions
contextNote.text: Verse 10 gives Jeremiah’s task in six verbs. Four of them tear down: uproot, tear down, destroy, overthrow. Two of them build: build and plant. That proportion matches the book that follows. The tearing down also comes first in the order. A young man from a village is set “over the nations.” These verbs return in 18:7–9, 24:6, and 31:28.

passages.title: Broken water tanks and abandoned loyalty
passages.summary: The LORD remembers Israel’s early devotion, like a bride who followed him in the desert. He asks what fault their fathers found in him. Priests, rulers, and prophets all turned away. No other nation has traded its gods, yet Israel traded its glory. The people left the spring of living water. They dug cracked tanks that hold no water. They run to Egypt and Assyria for help. They say to a tree, “You are my father.”
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me compares God’s help with living water. What makes the broken water tanks poor replacements?

contextNote.title: A water image explains failed dependence
contextNote.text: Verse 13 counts two wrongs. The people left a spring, and they dug cisterns. A spring flows on its own with fresh water. A cistern is a pit cut in rock to catch runoff. It takes hard labor, and its plaster cracks. So the people gave up a gift for a leaking thing they made. Verse 18 applies the picture to alliances and verses 27–28 to idols.

passages.title: An invitation to return
passages.summary: The LORD compares Judah to an unfaithful wife who still expects to return. In Josiah’s days he points to the northern kingdom. Israel was unfaithful and was sent away. Her sister Judah saw it and was not afraid. Judah returned to God only in pretense. So God calls Israel less guilty than Judah. He invites the north to return and only admit its guilt. He promises shepherds after his own heart and healing for the faithless.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies God’s invitation to return. What must Israel acknowledge before accepting that invitation?

contextNote.title: One nation's failure does not excuse another
contextNote.text: Judah watched the northern kingdom fall (2 Kings 17). Verse 8 says she saw it and learned nothing. Verse 10 says her return was “in pretense.” So verse 11 gives a surprising verdict. The nation with more warning is the more guilty. The invitation then goes to the north first (verse 12). Verse 13 sets one condition: “Only acknowledge your iniquity.”

passages.title: An approaching enemy and a ruined land
passages.summary: The LORD says Israel may return if she puts away her idols. Judah must break up its unplowed ground. A trumpet warns of disaster from the north. A lion has left its thicket to ruin the land. Jeremiah cries out in anguish at the sound of war. He sees the earth empty and the heavens without light. Mountains shake, people are gone, and the birds have fled. Yet the LORD says he will not make a full end.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah describe the land as empty and dark?

contextNote.title: Destruction reverses the language of creation
contextNote.text: Verse 23 echoes Genesis 1:2, where the earth was formless and empty. Jeremiah says “I saw” four times in verses 23–26. Light is gone, then mountains, people, birds, and gardens. The list runs creation backward. An invasion is described as the world being unmade. Verse 27 sets a limit on it. The land will be ruined, and it will not be the end.

passages.title: A search for justice
passages.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah to search Jerusalem for one person who does justice. If he finds one, God will pardon the city. Jeremiah thinks the poor simply do not know God’s way. He goes to the great men, and they too have broken free. A distant nation will come and devour their harvest. The people have eyes and do not see. Rich men grow fat and do not defend the orphan. Prophets lie, priests rule by their own authority, and the people love it.

lds.text: How does Jeremiah’s search change when he turns to powerful people?

contextNote.title: Knowledge of the law does not explain away injustice
contextNote.text: Jeremiah’s first guess in verse 4 is generous. Perhaps the poor do wrong because no one taught them. Verse 5 tests that idea on the educated. The leaders know the LORD’s way, and they have thrown it off. So lack of knowledge is not the cause. Verse 28 shows what this looks like in court. The orphan’s case is not heard, and the needy get no justice.

passages.title: Warnings that people refuse to hear
passages.summary: Jeremiah warns the people of Benjamin to flee Jerusalem. An army from the north prepares to attack. No one listens, for their ears are closed. Everyone is greedy, from the least to the greatest. Prophets and priests say “Peace, peace” when there is no peace. They do not know how to blush. God tells them to ask for the old paths and find rest. They answer that they will not walk in them.

lds.text: What damage follows the leaders’ promise of peace?

contextNote.title: Reassurance can conceal a wound
contextNote.text: Verse 14 uses a medical picture. The people have a serious wound. Their leaders dress it lightly and say all is well. Verse 13 gives the motive, which is gain. Verse 15 adds that they feel no shame. Verse 16 offers real rest on the old paths. The people refuse it in so many words.

passages.title: Temple worship and harm to neighbors
passages.summary: Jeremiah stands at the temple gate and speaks to those who enter. He tells them to change their ways. They must not trust the words “The LORD’s temple.” They must do justice and stop oppressing foreigners, orphans, and widows. They steal, murder, and worship Baal, then come and say they are safe. God asks whether his house has become a den of robbers. He tells them to remember what he did to Shiloh. They even burn their children in the valley of Hinnom.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects temple worship with daily conduct. Which actions must change before the people can safely remain?

contextNote.title: A temple can become a false source of safety
contextNote.text: Verse 4 quotes a phrase the people repeat three times. They treat the building as a guarantee. Verse 9 lists what they do during the week. It names theft, murder, adultery, false oaths, and other gods. Verse 11 calls the temple a robbers’ den, a hideout where thieves feel safe. Verse 12 points to Shiloh, an earlier holy place that fell (1 Samuel 4). Jesus quotes verse 11 in Matthew 21:13.

passages.title: Rejected warnings and grief for the wounded
passages.summary: The bones of Judah’s kings and priests will be spread under the sky. The LORD asks why the people never turn back. Even the stork knows its seasons. The people say they are wise and have the LORD’s law. Yet the scribes’ pen has turned it into a lie. Leaders say “Peace” when there is no peace. Jeremiah’s heart is sick for his people. He asks whether there is no balm in Gilead.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah ask about medicine when describing his people’s wounds?

contextNote.title: Possessing written law does not secure right judgment
contextNote.text: Verse 7 says migrating birds know their appointed times. God’s people do not know his requirements. Verse 8 quotes their defense. They have the written law, so they are wise. Jeremiah says the scribes’ handling has made it false. Readers differ on exactly what the scribes did. Verse 9 states the result: they reject the LORD’s word while holding it.

passages.title: Broken trust and reasons for grief
passages.summary: Jeremiah wishes his head were a spring of tears for his people. Neighbors deceive one another, and tongues are bent like bows. No one can trust a brother. The LORD will refine and test them. Jerusalem will become a heap of ruins. He calls for the mourning women, since death has climbed through the windows. The wise, the strong, and the rich must not boast. Let a person boast only in knowing the LORD.

lds.text: What replaces wealth, wisdom, and strength as a reason for praise?

contextNote.title: Knowing God receives a practical definition
contextNote.text: Verse 23 removes three common grounds for pride. Wisdom, strength, and riches are all set aside. Verse 24 leaves one. A person may boast in understanding and knowing the LORD. The verse then says what that knowledge contains. He acts with loving kindness, justice, and righteousness on the earth. Chapter 22:16 defines knowing God as defending the poor.

passages.title: Made idols and the living God
passages.summary: The LORD tells Israel not to learn the ways of the nations. A craftsman cuts a tree and decorates it with silver and gold. He fastens it with nails so that it will not fall. Such idols cannot speak or walk. No one is like the LORD, the living God. He made the earth by his power. Jeremiah mourns that his tent is destroyed. He admits that a person cannot direct his own steps.

lds.text: How does the need to carry an idol support Jeremiah’s argument?

contextNote.title: Craftsmanship and authority are different claims
contextNote.text: Verse 5 lists what the idol cannot do. It cannot speak, and it cannot move. Its worshipers must carry it. A god that depends on its people for transport offers them nothing. So the verse says not to fear it. It can do neither harm nor good. Verses 10 and 12–13 set the living God against it.

passages.title: A broken covenant and threats from Anathoth
passages.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah to proclaim the terms of the covenant. The fathers were told to obey when they left Egypt. They did not, and their children have returned to those sins. God tells Jeremiah not to pray for them. Then the LORD shows Jeremiah a plot against his life. He had been like a gentle lamb led to slaughter. The men of Anathoth tell him to stop prophesying or die. God says he will punish them.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Why does the threat from Anathoth make Jeremiah’s task harder?

contextNote.title: The speaker's own community tries to restrict his speech
contextNote.text: Anathoth is Jeremiah’s home village (1:1). Verse 21 says its men want him dead. They do not argue with his message. They forbid him to speak it. Verse 19 says he had not known of the plot until God showed him. Chapter 12:6 adds that his own brothers were involved. The first threat to this prophet comes from his neighbors.

passages.title: Jeremiah questions the success of wrongdoers
passages.summary: Jeremiah brings a case before the LORD. He asks why the wicked prosper and the faithless live at ease. He asks how long the land must mourn. God answers with a question. If running with men has tired him, how will he race horses? Even his own family has betrayed him. God says he has left his house and given his beloved to enemies. Yet he will later have compassion on the neighbors who harmed Israel.

lds.text: How does the warning about Jeremiah’s family answer his complaint?

contextNote.title: A complaint tests the gap between justice and experience
contextNote.text: Verse 1 opens like a lawsuit. Jeremiah first grants that the LORD is in the right. Then he argues anyway. His question is the one Job and Psalm 73 ask. God’s reply in verse 5 explains nothing. It says the road ahead is harder. An honest complaint is allowed, and it is answered with preparation.

passages.title: A ruined waistband and stubborn habits
passages.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah to buy a linen belt and wear it. Then he must hide it in a rock by the river. After many days he digs it up, and it is ruined. God says he will ruin Judah’s pride in the same way. As a belt clings to the waist, he made Israel cling to him. They would not listen. Jeremiah warns the king and the queen mother that their crowns will fall. He asks whether a leopard can change its spots.

lds.text: What does the waistband’s change explain about Judah’s broken loyalty?

contextNote.title: A close-fitting object represents a broken relationship
contextNote.text: A belt is worn close against the body. Verse 11 uses it for the bond God meant to have with his people. They were to be his name, praise, and glory. The picture is closeness, not only obedience. The belt is spoiled by being buried somewhere else. Judah’s ruin is the loss of that closeness. Verse 23 adds that long habit has made change hard.

passages.title: Drought and competing messages
passages.summary: A drought strikes Judah. Nobles send servants for water, and the cisterns are empty. The ground is cracked, and even the deer abandons her fawn. The people admit their sins and ask God to act for his name’s sake. God tells Jeremiah not to pray for them. Jeremiah says the prophets are promising peace. The LORD answers that he did not send those prophets. They and those who believe them will fall by sword and famine.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: How do the prophets’ promises differ from Jeremiah’s warning?

contextNote.title: Competing messages appear during visible scarcity
contextNote.text: Jeremiah speaks up for the people in verse 13. Other prophets have told them there will be no sword or famine. He suggests they have been misled. The LORD’s answer in verses 14–16 does not accept that excuse. He did not send those prophets, and their hearers share their end. The promise of “assured peace” comes during a drought anyone can see. Two messages are in the air, and events will show which is true.

passages.title: Jeremiah’s suffering and renewed task
passages.summary: The LORD says he would not relent even if Moses and Samuel pleaded. The people are assigned to death, sword, famine, and exile. Jeremiah laments that his mother bore him. Everyone curses him, though he has wronged no one. He found God’s words and ate them with joy. He sat alone because God’s hand was on him. He asks why his pain never ends. God tells him to return and promises to make him a bronze wall.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: What must Jeremiah change when God renews his charge?

contextNote.title: The prophet's complaint is part of his service
contextNote.text: In 2:13 the LORD called himself a spring of living water. In verse 18 Jeremiah turns that picture against him. He asks whether God will be like a stream that fails. It is a severe charge. God’s answer in verse 19 tells the prophet himself to “return.” Then he repeats the promise made at Jeremiah’s call (1:18–19). The complaint is corrected, and the book still keeps it.

passages.title: Missing celebrations and pursuing hunters
passages.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah not to marry or have children in this place. Parents and children there will die and lie unburied. He must not enter a house of mourning or comfort anyone. He must not enter a house of feasting. The sounds of weddings will stop. When people ask why, he must say they have left the LORD. Yet a day will come when God brings Israel back from the north. Nations will come and admit their fathers inherited lies.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me uses fishers and hunters to discuss gathering Israel. How does that lesson differ from the pursuit described in verses 16–18?

contextNote.title: Missing household rituals make coming loss visible
contextNote.text: Jeremiah receives three bans. He may not marry (verse 2), mourn (verse 5), or feast (verse 8). His own life becomes a sign of what is coming. The ordinary rites of grief and joy are about to stop for everyone. Verse 5 gives the reason for the second ban. God has withdrawn his peace, kindness, and mercy from this people. Chapter 15:17 shows how lonely this made the prophet.

passages.title: Trust, hidden motives, and the Sabbath
passages.summary: Judah’s sin is engraved on its heart with an iron pen. A person who trusts in human strength is like a shrub in the desert. A person who trusts the LORD is like a tree planted by water. The heart is more deceitful than anything, and the LORD searches it. Jeremiah asks God to heal him and to shame his persecutors. The LORD sends him to the city gates. The people must carry no loads on the Sabbath. If they obey, kings will keep entering those gates.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: How does the tree beside water remain fruitful during heat?

contextNote.title: The tree image allows difficulty within trust
contextNote.text: Verse 8 resembles Psalm 1:3 and adds something. Heat comes, and a year of drought comes. Trust does not keep the hard season away. The tree stays green because its roots reach the stream. The shrub in verse 6 cannot even see good when it arrives. Verse 9 then warns that the heart can deceive its owner. A person may be wrong about where his trust lies.

passages.title: A potter’s work and plots against Jeremiah
passages.summary: The LORD sends Jeremiah to a potter’s house. The clay pot is spoiled on the wheel, and the potter reshapes it. God says Israel is like clay in his hand. If he warns a nation and it turns from evil, he will relent. If he promises good and a nation does evil, he will withhold it. He calls Judah to turn back. The people answer that it is hopeless and they will follow their own plans. Then they plot against Jeremiah.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the potter’s work. What does the spoiled clay’s new form explain about changing conduct?

contextNote.title: Soft clay presents a future that can change
contextNote.text: The clay in verse 4 is still wet and on the wheel. The potter can make it again. Verses 7–10 draw a lesson that works in both directions. A warning can be withdrawn, and so can a promise. Verse 8 gives the first case: a nation turns, and God relents. The people reply in verse 12 that nothing can change. They use hopelessness as a reason to go on as before.

passages.title: A broken jar before the elders
passages.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah to buy a clay jar. He must take elders and senior priests to the valley of Hinnom. There he says the people have filled the place with innocent blood. They have burned their sons as offerings to Baal. The valley will be called the Valley of Slaughter. Jeremiah breaks the jar in front of them. God will break the city like a jar that cannot be mended. Jeremiah repeats the message in the temple court.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: How does the broken jar differ from the clay in chapter 18?

contextNote.title: A broken vessel changes the force of the earlier image
contextNote.text: Chapter 18 used soft clay that a potter could reshape. This chapter uses a finished jar that has been fired. Verse 11 says a broken jar “can’t be made whole again.” The time for reshaping can pass. Jeremiah acts this out before the nation’s leaders. He does it in the valley where children were burned (verse 5). The place and the audience are part of the message.

passages.title: Pashhur attacks Jeremiah
passages.summary: Pashhur, a chief officer of the temple, hears Jeremiah’s words. He has Jeremiah beaten and locked in the stocks. The next day Jeremiah gives him a new name: Terror on Every Side. Then Jeremiah complains to the LORD. He says God overpowered him, and he has become a joke. If he tries to keep silent, the word burns like fire in his bones. He praises the LORD as a mighty warrior. Then he curses the day he was born.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Jeremiah’s costly service. Why can he neither stop speaking nor escape his grief?

contextNote.title: Praise and anguish remain in the same voice
contextNote.text: Jeremiah is caught between two pains. When he speaks, people mock him (verse 8). When he holds back, verse 9 says a fire burns in his bones. He cannot keep it in. Verses 11–13 then speak with trust and praise. Verses 14–18 curse his birth, as Job did. The book places both in one voice and does not explain the change.

passages.title: Zedekiah asks for rescue
passages.summary: King Zedekiah sends two officials to Jeremiah. Babylon’s king is attacking, and they hope the LORD will work a wonder. Jeremiah answers that God himself will fight against the city. Its people will die of sword, famine, and disease. The king will be handed to Babylon. The people may choose life by surrendering. The royal house is told to give justice every morning. It must rescue the robbed from the oppressor.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: What answer challenges Zedekiah’s hope for a miraculous rescue?

contextNote.title: A request for rescue meets a demand for justice
contextNote.text: Zedekiah hopes for a rescue like the one in Hezekiah’s day (verse 2). Verse 5 says God’s outstretched hand is now against the city. Verse 12 then speaks to the royal house about its neglected work. A king held court in the morning. He was to rescue the person robbed by a stronger one. The king asks for a wonder and is told to do justice. The city’s safety is tied to the safety of its weakest people.

passages.title: Kings judged by their treatment of others
passages.summary: The LORD sends Jeremiah to the king’s house. The king must do justice and protect the foreigner, orphan, and widow. If not, the palace will become a ruin. One king has been carried off and will never return. Jehoiakim builds a grand house with unpaid labor. His father Josiah did justice and defended the poor. Jehoiakim will have a donkey’s burial. The young king Coniah will be thrown out like a broken pot.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah compare Jehoiakim’s cedar house with Josiah’s care for poor people?

contextNote.title: Royal buildings reveal how power treats workers
contextNote.text: Verse 13 accuses Jehoiakim of building with forced, unpaid labor. The law required prompt wages (Leviticus 19:13; Deuteronomy 24:14–15). Verse 15 asks whether cedar panels make a man a king. It then points to his father Josiah. Josiah ate and drank well and still did justice. Verse 16 says he judged the cause of the poor and needy. It adds, “Wasn’t this to know me?”

passages.title: Harmful leaders and prophets who promise peace
passages.summary: The LORD condemns the shepherds who scatter his flock. He will gather the remnant and raise a righteous Branch for David. That king will be called “The LORD our righteousness.” Jeremiah’s heart is broken because of the prophets. They commit adultery, live in lies, and encourage evildoers. They speak visions from their own minds. They tell those who despise God that all will be well. God says his word is like fire and like a hammer.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: What effect should a prophet’s words have on people’s conduct?

contextNote.title: A prophet's effect on conduct matters
contextNote.text: The false prophets claim to know God’s mind. Verse 18 asks who has really stood in his council. Verse 22 gives a test that anyone can apply. A prophet who had stood there would turn people from evil. These prophets do the opposite. Verse 14 says they strengthen the hands of evildoers. Verse 17 says they promise peace to people who despise the LORD.

passages.title: Two baskets of figs
passages.summary: Babylon has carried off King Jeconiah, the officials, and the craftsmen. The LORD shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs before the temple. One holds very good figs, and the other holds figs too bad to eat. The good figs are the exiles in Babylon. God will watch over them and bring them back. He will give them a heart to know him. The bad figs are King Zedekiah and those left in the land. They will become a horror to all kingdoms.

lds.text: How do the good figs challenge assumptions about those taken to Babylon?

contextNote.title: Remaining at home does not prove divine favor
contextNote.text: Those left in Jerusalem thought they were the favored ones (Ezekiel 11:15). The exiles looked like people God had thrown away. Verse 5 reverses that judgment. The exiles are the good figs. Verse 6 turns the hard verbs of 1:10 into promises. God will build and plant them. Verse 7 adds a gift they could not make: a heart to know him.

passages.title: Babylon’s rule and the cup of anger
passages.summary: In Jehoiakim’s fourth year Jeremiah speaks to all Judah. For twenty-three years he has warned them, and they have not listened. So the LORD will bring Nebuchadnezzar, his servant, against the land. The nations will serve Babylon’s king for seventy years. Then God will punish Babylon for its own guilt. Jeremiah takes a cup of wrath to the nations. Jerusalem drinks first, and Babylon’s king drinks last. The LORD will roar from on high against all the earth.

lds.text: Why does Babylon face judgment after serving God’s announced purpose?

contextNote.title: The conqueror also comes under judgment
contextNote.text: Verse 9 calls Babylon’s king “my servant.” Verse 12 says God will punish that king and nation. Being used by God is not the same as being approved. Babylon answers for its own wrongs. The seventy years set a limit of about a lifetime. The exile will be neither short nor endless. The cup in verses 18–26 starts with Jerusalem and ends with Babylon.

passages.title: Jeremiah faces a death charge
passages.summary: Early in Jehoiakim’s reign Jeremiah speaks in the temple court. He says the house will become like Shiloh unless the people change. Priests and prophets seize him and demand his death. Officials come and hold a hearing at the gate. Jeremiah says the LORD sent him and that he is in their hands. Some elders recall the prophet Micah. King Hezekiah did not kill Micah for a similar message. Another prophet, Uriah, was killed, but an official protects Jeremiah.

lds.text: How does the memory of Micah help Jeremiah when Uriah receives no protection?

contextNote.title: Earlier prophecy becomes evidence in a public hearing
contextNote.text: The elders quote Micah 3:12 from about a century earlier (verse 18). Prophecies were remembered and could be cited in court. Verse 19 draws the precedent. Hezekiah feared the LORD, prayed, and the disaster did not come. So a warning of ruin is an invitation to change. Verses 20–23 add a second case with the opposite end. Uriah was killed, and one official saved Jeremiah (verse 24).

passages.title: A yoke warns against rebellion
passages.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah to make a yoke and wear it on his neck. He sends word to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon. Their envoys are visiting King Zedekiah in Jerusalem. God made the earth and gives it to whom he chooses. He has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar for a time. Any nation that will not serve Babylon will be destroyed. Jeremiah tells Zedekiah to accept the yoke and live. He warns the priests that the temple vessels will not soon return.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah treat accepting the yoke as a way to survive?

contextNote.title: An object challenges the hope for immediate independence
contextNote.text: Foreign envoys have gathered in Jerusalem (verse 3). They seem to be planning a revolt against Babylon. Jeremiah walks among them wearing a wooden yoke. Verse 12 gives the king his advice: serve Babylon and live. It sounds like disloyalty to his own country. His ground is in verses 5–6: the Creator has assigned this rule. Verse 7 adds that Babylon’s own time will also end.

passages.title: Hananiah breaks the yoke
passages.summary: In the same year the prophet Hananiah speaks in the temple. He says the LORD has broken Babylon’s yoke. Within two years the vessels and the exiled king will return. Jeremiah answers that he wishes it were so. Yet he says a prophet of peace is proved only when his word comes true. Hananiah takes the yoke from Jeremiah’s neck and breaks it. Jeremiah goes away. Later he tells Hananiah that he will die that year, and he does.

lds.text: What does Jeremiah’s iron yoke answer in Hananiah’s promise?

contextNote.title: Breaking a symbol does not settle a dispute
contextNote.text: Both prophets speak in the LORD’s name in the same place. Jeremiah first wishes that Hananiah were right (verse 6). Verse 9 then gives the test. Earlier prophets warned of war, so a promise of peace must be proved. Time will show who was sent. Hananiah breaks the yoke, and Jeremiah simply leaves (verses 10–11). A dramatic act does not settle the dispute.

passages.title: A letter to people in exile
passages.summary: Jeremiah sends a letter from Jerusalem to the exiles in Babylon. The LORD tells them to build houses and plant gardens. They should marry and have children. They should seek the peace of the city and pray for it. Prophets who promise a quick return are lying. After seventy years God will bring them back. He has plans for their peace and a future with hope. Jeremiah also answers a man who wrote from Babylon against him.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah tell captives to pray for the city that holds them?

contextNote.title: A promise of return includes ordinary life in exile
contextNote.text: The letter names homes, gardens, marriages, and the city’s peace. Verse 7 asks the exiles to pray for Babylon, their captor. Their own welfare is bound up with that city’s welfare. Verse 5 uses “build” and “plant” from 1:10 for a foreign land. An Egyptian scribe’s palette shows the tools behind such a letter. The promise of verse 11 comes with a date of seventy years. Most who heard it would live out their lives in exile.

passages.title: Healing after national suffering
passages.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah to write his words in a book. Days are coming when he will restore Israel and Judah. There is a cry of terror, and it is a time of trouble for Jacob. Yet Jacob will be saved out of it. God will break the yoke from their necks. Their wound seems beyond cure, and their allies have forgotten them. God will restore their health and heal their wounds. The city will be rebuilt, and songs of thanks will rise from it.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: What does God promise people whom others call abandoned?

contextNote.title: Healing answers both injury and exclusion
contextNote.text: Verse 12 calls the wound incurable. Verse 14 says God himself struck the blow. Verse 17 then says the same God will heal it. The verse gives a reason drawn from an insult. Others called Zion an outcast that no one cares for. God answers the injury and the shame together. The one whom nobody seeks is sought by him.

passages.title: Return and a law written in hearts
passages.summary: The LORD says he has loved Israel with an everlasting love. He will rebuild her, and she will dance again. He will gather the scattered from the north, with the blind and the lame. Rachel weeps for her children, and God tells her there is hope. He will watch over his people to build and to plant. He will make a new covenant with Israel and Judah. He will write his law on their hearts. He will forgive their wrongs and remember their sin no more.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies God’s law written in hearts. How does the new agreement differ from the one the people broke?

contextNote.title: The covenant promise changes where the law resides
contextNote.text: The first covenant was written on stone tablets (Exodus 31:18). Chapter 17:1 said Judah’s sin was engraved on its heart. Verse 33 puts God’s law in that same place. Verse 32 says the people broke the earlier covenant. The new one changes where the law lives. Verse 34 rests it all on forgiveness. Hebrews 8:8–12 quotes this passage in full.

passages.title: Jeremiah buys a field during the siege
passages.summary: Jerusalem is under siege, and Jeremiah is held in the court of the guard. His cousin comes and asks him to buy a field in Anathoth. Jeremiah weighs out seventeen shekels of silver. He signs and seals the deed before witnesses. He gives the deeds to Baruch to store in a clay jar. The LORD says houses and fields will again be bought in this land. Jeremiah prays and asks why he should buy land the enemy holds. God answers that nothing is too hard for him.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies God’s lasting promises. Why does Jeremiah preserve purchase deeds while Jerusalem faces capture?

contextNote.title: A land purchase gives hope a material form
contextNote.text: The field lies in territory the enemy already controls. On any market it is worthless. Jeremiah still follows every legal step (verses 10–12). Verse 14 orders the deeds kept in a jar “that they may last many days.” The wait will be long. The purchase puts money behind the promise in verse 15. The tablet offers an earlier regional comparison for recording land sales.

passages.title: Healing, a just ruler, and renewed worship
passages.summary: The LORD speaks to Jeremiah a second time in the court of the guard. Houses have been torn down for defense and filled with the dead. God will bring health and healing to the city. He will cleanse and forgive the people. The sounds of joy will be heard again in the empty streets. Shepherds will again count their flocks. God will raise a righteous Branch for David. His covenant with David is as sure as day and night.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me identifies the righteous Branch with Jesus Christ. What actions does the promised ruler perform?

contextNote.title: Restoration receives the sounds of ordinary life
contextNote.text: Three times Jeremiah said the bridegroom and bride would fall silent (7:34; 16:9). Verse 11 brings those very sounds back. Restoration is described in ordinary terms. People hold weddings and sing thanks in the LORD’s house. The song they sing is the refrain of Psalm 136. Verse 13 adds shepherds counting sheep. A healed land is one where daily life goes on.

passages.title: Freed servants are forced back into slavery
passages.summary: Babylon’s army is attacking Jerusalem and the last towns of Judah. Jeremiah tells King Zedekiah the city will fall. Zedekiah and the people make a covenant to free their Hebrew slaves. They release them and then force them back. The LORD recalls his law that slaves go free in the seventh year. The people did right for a moment and then profaned his name. So God proclaims a “liberty” for them to sword, disease, and famine. The Babylonian army will return and burn the city.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Why does forcing freed servants back into slavery break the agreement?

contextNote.title: A public promise loses meaning when power reverses it
contextNote.text: Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12 required freedom after six years of service. The owners freed their slaves while the siege pressed them (verses 8–10). Verse 21 shows the army had pulled back for a time. Verse 16 says the owners then took the people back. They had sworn the release in the temple, so they profaned God’s name. A promise made under fear was dropped when the fear eased. Verse 17 turns their word “liberty” against them.

passages.title: The Rechabites refuse wine
passages.summary: In Jehoiakim’s days the LORD sends Jeremiah to the Rechabite family. Jeremiah brings them into a temple room and offers them wine. They refuse, since their ancestor Jonadab forbade it. He also told them to live in tents and plant no vineyards. They have obeyed in everything. The LORD asks Judah why it will not learn from this. A family obeys a dead ancestor, and Judah ignores its God. He promises that Jonadab’s family will always have someone to serve him.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: How does the Rechabites’ refusal challenge Judah’s response to God?

contextNote.title: A family tradition creates a comparison, not a universal rule
contextNote.text: Jonadab lived in the time of King Jehu, long before (2 Kings 10:15). His family still keeps his rules. Verse 14 sets that beside Judah’s record. God has spoken again and again, and Judah has not listened. The argument goes from the lesser to the greater. The LORD does not tell Judah to give up wine or houses. He praises the Rechabites’ loyalty, not their particular rules.

passages.title: Jehoiakim burns the scroll
passages.summary: In Jehoiakim’s fourth year the LORD tells Jeremiah to write his words on a scroll. Baruch writes as Jeremiah speaks. Baruch reads the scroll in the temple on a fast day. Officials hear it, are afraid, and tell Baruch and Jeremiah to hide. The scroll is read to the king beside a winter fire. He cuts off each part as it is read and burns it. He orders their arrest, but the LORD hides them. Jeremiah dictates the scroll again, with many words added.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies scripture that calls people to change. How does Jehoiakim’s response differ from the officials’ fear?

contextNote.title: Destroying a copy does not end the message
contextNote.text: The scroll moves through writing, public reading, court officials, and the king. Baruch writes it with ink (verse 18); a scribe’s palette held such ink. The officials tremble when they hear it (verse 16). The king cuts and burns it column by column (verse 23). Verse 24 notes that he did not tear his clothes. His father Josiah did tear his at a reading (2 Kings 22:11). Verse 32 says the second scroll was longer than the first.

passages.title: A false charge sends Jeremiah to prison
passages.summary: Zedekiah is king, and no one listens to Jeremiah. The king asks him to pray for the city. Egypt’s army marches out, and the Babylonians withdraw from Jerusalem. Jeremiah says they will return and burn the city. He tries to leave for his family land in Benjamin. A guard arrests him as a deserter. He is beaten and kept in a dungeon for many days. The king questions him in secret and moves him to the court of the guard.
passages.uncertainty: Lines join the places Jeremiah names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies the cost of following prophetic counsel. Why does Zedekiah seek Jeremiah’s answer secretly?

contextNote.title: A temporary change in the war encourages a false conclusion
contextNote.text: The siege has lifted, and hope rises in the city. Verse 9 warns the people not to deceive themselves. The Babylonians “will not depart.” Verse 10 makes the point in an extreme form. Even an army of wounded men would rise and burn the city. A short change in the war proves nothing. Jeremiah’s advice to surrender also makes the desertion charge easy to believe (verse 13).

passages.title: Ebedmelech rescues Jeremiah
passages.summary: Officials hear Jeremiah say that those who surrender will live. They tell the king he is weakening the soldiers. The king says he cannot stop them. They lower Jeremiah into a cistern, and he sinks in the mud. Ebedmelech, an Ethiopian servant of the palace, tells the king. With thirty men he pulls Jeremiah out with ropes padded by old rags. The king meets Jeremiah in secret and is urged to surrender. He is too afraid to do it.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies Ebedmelech’s courage. What risks does he accept when he asks the king to rescue Jeremiah?

contextNote.title: Practical care answers danger that official power created
contextNote.text: The king gives Jeremiah up in verse 5, saying he can do nothing. A foreigner who serves in the palace acts in his place. Ebedmelech speaks to the king in public at the gate (verses 7–9). Verse 11 records where he found old rags and worn clothes. Verse 12 says they were to pad the ropes under Jeremiah’s arms. He thinks of a starved man’s skin. Chapter 39:15–18 gives him the LORD’s promise of safety.

passages.title: Jerusalem falls and Jeremiah is spared
passages.summary: After a siege of a year and a half the wall of Jerusalem is breached. Babylon’s officers sit in the Middle Gate. Zedekiah flees at night and is caught near Jericho. His sons are killed in front of him, and he is blinded. The city is burned, and its walls are broken down. Most of the people are taken to Babylon. The poorest are left behind and given vineyards and fields. Jeremiah is released, and Ebedmelech receives a promise of life.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies choices made during danger. How does Ebedmelech’s response differ from Zedekiah’s earlier fear?

contextNote.title: The city's fall affects people in unequal ways
contextNote.text: The chapter gives very different ends to different people. The king loses his sons and his sight (verses 6–7). The prophet is freed on Babylon’s orders (verses 11–14). The Ethiopian is promised his life (verses 16–18). Verse 10 says the poor, who owned nothing, received land. The text reports this and gives no motive for it. Jeremiah had charged the rich with seizing others’ goods (5:27–28; 22:13).

passages.title: Gedaliah governs the remaining people
passages.summary: The captain of the guard frees Jeremiah and lets him choose where to live. Jeremiah goes to Gedaliah, the governor Babylon appointed at Mizpah. Judah’s scattered army officers come to Gedaliah. He tells them to serve Babylon and it will go well. They should gather wine, summer fruit, and oil. Jews return from Moab, Ammon, and Edom and bring in a large harvest. An officer warns Gedaliah that a man named Ishmael plans to kill him. Gedaliah does not believe it.

lds.text: Why does Johanan think Ishmael’s plan threatens everyone gathered around Gedaliah?

contextNote.title: Harvest work offers a fragile recovery after conquest
contextNote.text: Gedaliah’s plan in verse 10 is simple. He will deal with the Babylonians, and the people will farm. They should gather the harvest and live in their towns. Verses 11–12 show it working, as refugees return to a good crop. The recovery depends on one man. Verse 16 shows him refusing to believe a warning. In verses 2–3 a Babylonian officer states Jeremiah’s own message.

passages.title: Ishmael kills Gedaliah and takes captives
passages.summary: Ishmael, a man of the royal family, comes to Mizpah with ten men. They eat with Gedaliah and then kill him and those with him. The next day Ishmael murders seventy pilgrims on their way to the temple. He throws the bodies into a cistern. He takes the people of Mizpah captive and heads for Ammon. Johanan and the other officers catch him at Gibeon. The captives are freed, and Ishmael escapes. The survivors camp near Bethlehem, ready to go to Egypt.

lds.text: How do Ishmael’s killings change the survivors’ plans for staying in Judah?

contextNote.title: A local killing changes the survivors' political choices
contextNote.text: The murder happens at a shared meal (verses 1–2). One killing ends the recovery described in chapter 40. Verse 18 gives the survivors’ reasoning. Babylon appointed Gedaliah, and Babylon will blame everyone for his death. Fear now drives their choices. Verse 5 shows pilgrims from the north still bringing offerings to a ruined temple. They are among the dead.

passages.title: Survivors ask for guidance
passages.summary: The officers and all the people come to Jeremiah. They ask him to pray that the LORD will show them the way. They promise to obey, whether the answer is pleasant or not. After ten days the word comes. If they stay in the land, God will build them up and plant them. They need not fear the king of Babylon. If they go to Egypt, the sword and famine will follow them there. Jeremiah says they deceived themselves when they asked.

lds.text: What part of the survivors’ promise becomes difficult when Jeremiah gives the answer?

contextNote.title: A promise to obey is tested by an unwanted answer
contextNote.text: Verse 6 is a promise made before the answer is known. The people will obey “whether it is good, or whether it is bad.” They had already camped on the road to Egypt (41:17). Verse 7 makes them wait ten days. The answer goes against the plan they had formed. Verse 10 offers the building and planting of 1:10. Verse 20 says they misled themselves when they asked.

passages.title: The survivors reject the answer
passages.summary: The officers tell Jeremiah he is lying. They say Baruch has turned him against them. They lead all the people into Egypt, with Jeremiah and Baruch. They settle at Tahpanhes. There the LORD tells Jeremiah to bury large stones at the entrance to Pharaoh’s house. Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne over those stones. He will strike Egypt and burn the houses of its gods.

lds.text: How does blaming Baruch help the leaders reject Jeremiah’s message?

contextNote.title: An accusation replaces an answer to the warning
contextNote.text: The people promised to obey any answer (42:6). In verse 2 they call the answer a lie. Verse 3 gives their way out. They do not address the warning itself. They accuse the scribe Baruch of hidden motives. Blaming a third person lets them reject the message. Jeremiah is taken to the very place he warned against, and he keeps speaking there.

passages.title: A dispute about the queen of the sky
passages.summary: The LORD’s word comes to the Jews living across Egypt. They have seen Jerusalem ruined because of offerings to other gods. Jeremiah asks why they repeat that sin in Egypt. The men and women answer that they will not listen. They will keep burning incense to the queen of the sky. When they did so in Judah, they had food and safety. Since they stopped, they have lacked everything. Jeremiah answers that the LORD remembered those offerings, and events will show whose word stands.

lds.text: How do the women and Jeremiah explain the lost food and peace differently?

contextNote.title: The dispute concerns the remembered cause of disaster
contextNote.text: Both sides argue from the same events. The people say trouble began when they stopped their offerings (verse 18). Jeremiah says trouble came because they made them (verses 21–23). Each reads the past as proof. Verse 17 shows the people appealing to their fathers and kings. The dispute is about the remembered cause of a disaster. Verse 28 leaves the test to the outcome.

passages.title: Baruch receives a promise of survival
passages.summary: This short word is for Baruch, Jeremiah’s scribe. It dates from the year he wrote the scroll. Baruch has said that the LORD added sorrow to his pain. He is worn out and finds no rest. The LORD says he is tearing down what he built across the whole land. He asks whether Baruch seeks great things for himself. Baruch should not seek them. He will keep his life wherever he goes.

lds.text: What does Baruch receive instead of the greatness he seeks?

contextNote.title: A scribe's private hopes meet a public crisis
contextNote.text: Baruch came from a family of officials; his brother served the king (51:59). He could have hoped for a career. Verse 4 puts God’s own loss first. God is breaking down what he himself built and planted. Against that, verse 5 asks about Baruch’s private hopes. Personal ambition is out of scale in such a time. He is promised one thing: his life.

passages.title: Egypt’s armies face defeat
passages.summary: This is the first of Jeremiah’s messages about foreign nations. Egypt’s army is defeated at Carchemish by the king of Babylon. Its soldiers are terrified and fall back. Egypt rose like the Nile and said it would cover the earth. No medicine will heal it. A second message says Nebuchadnezzar will invade Egypt itself. Pharaoh is called a loud noise who missed his moment. Afterward Egypt will be lived in again, and Jacob need not fear.

lds.text: How does Egypt’s boast differ from the soldiers’ flight?

contextNote.title: A river image exposes the gap between boast and outcome
contextNote.text: The Nile’s yearly flood was Egypt’s strength and pride. Verse 8 uses it as a picture of the army. Egypt says it will rise and cover the earth. Verses 5–6 have already shown the soldiers running. The boast and the outcome stand side by side. Verse 17 gives Pharaoh a mocking nickname. Verse 26 still says Egypt will be inhabited again.

passages.title: A warning against the Philistines
passages.summary: This message concerns the Philistines. Waters rise from the north and become an overflowing flood. People cry out at the sound of horses and chariots. Fathers are too weak to turn back for their children. Tyre and Sidon lose their last helpers. Gaza and Ashkelon are silenced. A voice asks how long the LORD’s sword will keep striking. The answer is that the LORD has given it an order.

lds.text: Why does the passage ask the sword to rest?

contextNote.title: A question asks how long violence will continue
contextNote.text: Verse 6 speaks to the sword itself. A voice asks how long before it will be quiet. It begs the sword to go back into its sheath. Verse 7 answers that it cannot rest while it has orders. The message is against an old enemy of Israel. It still contains a cry for the killing to stop. Verse 3 shows the cost: fathers who cannot help their children.

passages.title: Moab’s pride and suffering
passages.summary: This long message concerns Moab. Its towns are named one by one as they fall. Its god Chemosh goes into exile with his priests. Moab has been at ease since its youth, like wine left undisturbed. It mocked Israel and was very proud. The speaker wails for Moab and weeps for its vineyards. Joy and gladness are gone from its fields. Yet the LORD will restore Moab’s fortunes in the last days.

lds.text: How does the mourning for Moab complicate the warning against its pride?

contextNote.title: Grief remains beside the charge against Moab
contextNote.text: Verse 29 states the charge against Moab: great pride. Verse 27 adds that it laughed at Israel. Then verse 31 says, “I will wail for Moab.” The voice that judges also mourns. Verse 36 says the speaker’s heart moans like a flute. Judgment and grief come from the same mouth. Verse 47 ends the chapter with a promise of restoration.

passages.title: Warnings against neighboring peoples
passages.summary: This chapter gathers messages about five peoples. Ammon trusted in its treasures and will see its capital ruined. Edom trusted in its wisdom and its high cliffs. Damascus grows weak, and its young men fall in the streets. The desert tribes of Kedar lose their tents and camels. Elam’s bow is broken, and its people are scattered. Ammon and Elam are promised restoration afterward. God says he will keep Edom’s orphans alive.

lds.text: Which kinds of protection fail in these warnings?

contextNote.title: Different neighbors receive different endings
contextNote.text: Each people in this chapter relied on something different. Ammon had treasure and fertile valleys (verse 4). Edom had wisdom and cliffs (verses 7 and 16). Damascus had fame, Kedar had distance, and Elam had the bow. Every one of these protections fails. The endings are not the same. Ammon and Elam are restored, and Edom’s orphans are kept (verses 6, 11, 39).

passages.title: Babylon faces judgment
passages.summary: This message announces the fall of Babylon. Its gods are put to shame, and a nation from the north attacks. Israel and Judah come weeping and ask the way to Zion. They have been lost sheep, misled by their shepherds. Their enemies said harming them was no crime, since they had sinned. Assyria devoured Israel, and Babylon gnawed its bones. God will punish Babylon as he punished Assyria. The hammer of the whole earth is broken.

lds.text: Why does Babylon remain responsible after serving as an instrument of judgment?

contextNote.title: Being used in judgment does not excuse violence
contextNote.text: Verse 7 quotes the enemies’ defense. Israel sinned against the LORD, so those who devoured it are “not guilty.” They borrow the prophets’ own teaching to excuse themselves. The chapter rejects that excuse. Verse 11 says Babylon rejoiced as it plundered. Verse 29 says it was proud against the LORD. Being the means of judgment did not make its cruelty innocent.

passages.title: A scroll marks Babylon’s announced fall
passages.summary: The LORD will send a destroying wind against Babylon. Babylon was a golden cup that made the whole earth drunk. Now it falls suddenly, and its wound cannot be healed. The LORD made the earth by his power, and idols are nothing. Zion says Nebuchadnezzar swallowed her like a monster. Babylon’s thick walls will be leveled. Jeremiah writes all this in a scroll and gives it to an officer named Seraiah. Seraiah must read it in Babylon and sink it in the Euphrates.
passages.uncertainty: Points show the places this chapter names. A line joins two places when the text gives both ends of a trip.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah tell Seraiah to sink the scroll after reading it?

contextNote.title: Reading and sinking make a message into a witnessed act
contextNote.text: Verse 59 dates this to Zedekiah’s fourth year. In that same period Jeremiah told the exiles to pray for Babylon (29:7). The exiles should seek the city’s peace, and its fall is already written. Jeremiah wrote this in a book (verse 60); the palette shows a scribe’s tools. Seraiah is to read the scroll aloud in Babylon. A stone then sends the scroll beneath the river’s surface. Verse 64 explains the act: Babylon will sink and not rise.

passages.title: Jerusalem’s destruction and Jehoiachin’s release
passages.summary: This last chapter retells the fall of Jerusalem. Zedekiah rebels, and Babylon besieges the city until the food is gone. The wall is breached, and the king is caught and blinded. The temple, the palace, and the houses are burned. The bronze pillars and vessels of the temple are carried away. The chief priests and officials are executed. The numbers of the exiles are listed. Years later the king of Babylon frees Jehoiachin and feeds him at his table.

lds.text: What changes for Jehoiachin, and what losses remain unchanged?

contextNote.title: The appendix keeps a surviving king beside an unrepaired loss
contextNote.text: Chapter 51:64 said Jeremiah’s words ended there. This chapter adds history that matches 2 Kings 25. It shows that the city fell as he had said. Verses 17–23 list the temple’s bronze piece by piece as it is taken. Nothing is said to repair that loss. Verse 31 then reports a small mercy to a captive king. The book ends with a ruined temple and a living heir of David.

events.title: Jeremiah receives his call
events.summary: Jeremiah is a priest’s son from the village of Anathoth. The LORD’s word comes to him in the days of King Josiah. God says he knew Jeremiah before he was formed in the womb. He has appointed him a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah answers that he is only a youth and cannot speak. The LORD touches his mouth and puts words in it. Jeremiah sees an almond branch and a boiling pot tilted from the north. God promises to make him like a fortified city against the whole land.
events.detail: Verse 10 gives Jeremiah’s task in six verbs. Four of them tear down: uproot, tear down, destroy, overthrow. Two of them build: build and plant. That proportion matches the book that follows. The tearing down also comes first in the order. A young man from a village is set “over the nations.” These verbs return in 18:7–9, 24:6, and 31:28.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me teaches that God knew Jeremiah before birth. How does God answer Jeremiah’s fear about speaking?

events.title: Broken water tanks and abandoned loyalty
events.summary: The LORD remembers Israel’s early devotion, like a bride who followed him in the desert. He asks what fault their fathers found in him. Priests, rulers, and prophets all turned away. No other nation has traded its gods, yet Israel traded its glory. The people left the spring of living water. They dug cracked tanks that hold no water. They run to Egypt and Assyria for help. They say to a tree, “You are my father.”
events.detail: Verse 13 counts two wrongs. The people left a spring, and they dug cisterns. A spring flows on its own with fresh water. A cistern is a pit cut in rock to catch runoff. It takes hard labor, and its plaster cracks. So the people gave up a gift for a leaking thing they made. Verse 18 applies the picture to alliances and verses 27–28 to idols.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me compares God’s help with living water. What makes the broken water tanks poor replacements?

events.title: An invitation to return
events.summary: The LORD compares Judah to an unfaithful wife who still expects to return. In Josiah’s days he points to the northern kingdom. Israel was unfaithful and was sent away. Her sister Judah saw it and was not afraid. Judah returned to God only in pretense. So God calls Israel less guilty than Judah. He invites the north to return and only admit its guilt. He promises shepherds after his own heart and healing for the faithless.
events.detail: Judah watched the northern kingdom fall (2 Kings 17). Verse 8 says she saw it and learned nothing. Verse 10 says her return was “in pretense.” So verse 11 gives a surprising verdict. The nation with more warning is the more guilty. The invitation then goes to the north first (verse 12). Verse 13 sets one condition: “Only acknowledge your iniquity.”

lds.text: Come, Follow Me studies God’s invitation to return. What must Israel acknowledge before accepting that invitation?

events.title: An approaching enemy and a ruined land
events.summary: The LORD says Israel may return if she puts away her idols. Judah must break up its unplowed ground. A trumpet warns of disaster from the north. A lion has left its thicket to ruin the land. Jeremiah cries out in anguish at the sound of war. He sees the earth empty and the heavens without light. Mountains shake, people are gone, and the birds have fled. Yet the LORD says he will not make a full end.
events.detail: Verse 23 echoes Genesis 1:2, where the earth was formless and empty. Jeremiah says “I saw” four times in verses 23–26. Light is gone, then mountains, people, birds, and gardens. The list runs creation backward. An invasion is described as the world being unmade. Verse 27 sets a limit on it. The land will be ruined, and it will not be the end.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah describe the land as empty and dark?

events.title: A search for justice
events.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah to search Jerusalem for one person who does justice. If he finds one, God will pardon the city. Jeremiah thinks the poor simply do not know God’s way. He goes to the great men, and they too have broken free. A distant nation will come and devour their harvest. The people have eyes and do not see. Rich men grow fat and do not defend the orphan. Prophets lie, priests rule by their own authority, and the people love it.
events.detail: Jeremiah’s first guess in verse 4 is generous. Perhaps the poor do wrong because no one taught them. Verse 5 tests that idea on the educated. The leaders know the LORD’s way, and they have thrown it off. So lack of knowledge is not the cause. Verse 28 shows what this looks like in court. The orphan’s case is not heard, and the needy get no justice.

lds.text: How does Jeremiah’s search change when he turns to powerful people?

events.title: Warnings that people refuse to hear
events.summary: Jeremiah warns the people of Benjamin to flee Jerusalem. An army from the north prepares to attack. No one listens, for their ears are closed. Everyone is greedy, from the least to the greatest. Prophets and priests say “Peace, peace” when there is no peace. They do not know how to blush. God tells them to ask for the old paths and find rest. They answer that they will not walk in them.
events.detail: Verse 14 uses a medical picture. The people have a serious wound. Their leaders dress it lightly and say all is well. Verse 13 gives the motive, which is gain. Verse 15 adds that they feel no shame. Verse 16 offers real rest on the old paths. The people refuse it in so many words.

lds.text: What damage follows the leaders’ promise of peace?

events.title: Temple worship and harm to neighbors
events.summary: Jeremiah stands at the temple gate and speaks to those who enter. He tells them to change their ways. They must not trust the words “The LORD’s temple.” They must do justice and stop oppressing foreigners, orphans, and widows. They steal, murder, and worship Baal, then come and say they are safe. God asks whether his house has become a den of robbers. He tells them to remember what he did to Shiloh. They even burn their children in the valley of Hinnom.
events.detail: Verse 4 quotes a phrase the people repeat three times. They treat the building as a guarantee. Verse 9 lists what they do during the week. It names theft, murder, adultery, false oaths, and other gods. Verse 11 calls the temple a robbers’ den, a hideout where thieves feel safe. Verse 12 points to Shiloh, an earlier holy place that fell (1 Samuel 4). Jesus quotes verse 11 in Matthew 21:13.

lds.text: Come, Follow Me connects temple worship with daily conduct. Which actions must change before the people can safely remain?

events.title: Rejected warnings and grief for the wounded
events.summary: The bones of Judah’s kings and priests will be spread under the sky. The LORD asks why the people never turn back. Even the stork knows its seasons. The people say they are wise and have the LORD’s law. Yet the scribes’ pen has turned it into a lie. Leaders say “Peace” when there is no peace. Jeremiah’s heart is sick for his people. He asks whether there is no balm in Gilead.
events.detail: Verse 7 says migrating birds know their appointed times. God’s people do not know his requirements. Verse 8 quotes their defense. They have the written law, so they are wise. Jeremiah says the scribes’ handling has made it false. Readers differ on exactly what the scribes did. Verse 9 states the result: they reject the LORD’s word while holding it.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah ask about medicine when describing his people’s wounds?

events.title: Broken trust and reasons for grief
events.summary: Jeremiah wishes his head were a spring of tears for his people. Neighbors deceive one another, and tongues are bent like bows. No one can trust a brother. The LORD will refine and test them. Jerusalem will become a heap of ruins. He calls for the mourning women, since death has climbed through the windows. The wise, the strong, and the rich must not boast. Let a person boast only in knowing the LORD.
events.detail: Verse 23 removes three common grounds for pride. Wisdom, strength, and riches are all set aside. Verse 24 leaves one. A person may boast in understanding and knowing the LORD. The verse then says what that knowledge contains. He acts with loving kindness, justice, and righteousness on the earth. Chapter 22:16 defines knowing God as defending the poor.

lds.text: What replaces wealth, wisdom, and strength as a reason for praise?

events.title: Made idols and the living God
events.summary: The LORD tells Israel not to learn the ways of the nations. A craftsman cuts a tree and decorates it with silver and gold. He fastens it with nails so that it will not fall. Such idols cannot speak or walk. No one is like the LORD, the living God. He made the earth by his power. Jeremiah mourns that his tent is destroyed. He admits that a person cannot direct his own steps.
events.detail: Verse 5 lists what the idol cannot do. It cannot speak, and it cannot move. Its worshipers must carry it. A god that depends on its people for transport offers them nothing. So the verse says not to fear it. It can do neither harm nor good. Verses 10 and 12–13 set the living God against it.

lds.text: How does the need to carry an idol support Jeremiah’s argument?

events.title: A broken covenant and threats from Anathoth
events.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah to proclaim the terms of the covenant. The fathers were told to obey when they left Egypt. They did not, and their children have returned to those sins. God tells Jeremiah not to pray for them. Then the LORD shows Jeremiah a plot against his life. He had been like a gentle lamb led to slaughter. The men of Anathoth tell him to stop prophesying or die. God says he will punish them.
events.detail: Anathoth is Jeremiah’s home village (1:1). Verse 21 says its men want him dead. They do not argue with his message. They forbid him to speak it. Verse 19 says he had not known of the plot until God showed him. Chapter 12:6 adds that his own brothers were involved. The first threat to this prophet comes from his neighbors.

lds.text: Why does the threat from Anathoth make Jeremiah’s task harder?

events.title: Jeremiah questions the success of wrongdoers
events.summary: Jeremiah brings a case before the LORD. He asks why the wicked prosper and the faithless live at ease. He asks how long the land must mourn. God answers with a question. If running with men has tired him, how will he race horses? Even his own family has betrayed him. God says he has left his house and given his beloved to enemies. Yet he will later have compassion on the neighbors who harmed Israel.
events.detail: Verse 1 opens like a lawsuit. Jeremiah first grants that the LORD is in the right. Then he argues anyway. His question is the one Job and Psalm 73 ask. God’s reply in verse 5 explains nothing. It says the road ahead is harder. An honest complaint is allowed, and it is answered with preparation.

lds.text: How does the warning about Jeremiah’s family answer his complaint?

events.title: A ruined waistband and stubborn habits
events.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah to buy a linen belt and wear it. Then he must hide it in a rock by the river. After many days he digs it up, and it is ruined. God says he will ruin Judah’s pride in the same way. As a belt clings to the waist, he made Israel cling to him. They would not listen. Jeremiah warns the king and the queen mother that their crowns will fall. He asks whether a leopard can change its spots.
events.detail: A belt is worn close against the body. Verse 11 uses it for the bond God meant to have with his people. They were to be his name, praise, and glory. The picture is closeness, not only obedience. The belt is spoiled by being buried somewhere else. Judah’s ruin is the loss of that closeness. Verse 23 adds that long habit has made change hard.

lds.text: What does the waistband’s change explain about Judah’s broken loyalty?

events.title: Drought and competing messages
events.summary: A drought strikes Judah. Nobles send servants for water, and the cisterns are empty. The ground is cracked, and even the deer abandons her fawn. The people admit their sins and ask God to act for his name’s sake. God tells Jeremiah not to pray for them. Jeremiah says the prophets are promising peace. The LORD answers that he did not send those prophets. They and those who believe them will fall by sword and famine.
events.detail: Jeremiah speaks up for the people in verse 13. Other prophets have told them there will be no sword or famine. He suggests they have been misled. The LORD’s answer in verses 14–16 does not accept that excuse. He did not send those prophets, and their hearers share their end. The promise of “assured peace” comes during a drought anyone can see. Two messages are in the air, and events will show which is true.

lds.text: How do the prophets’ promises differ from Jeremiah’s warning?

events.title: Jeremiah’s suffering and renewed task
events.summary: The LORD says he would not relent even if Moses and Samuel pleaded. The people are assigned to death, sword, famine, and exile. Jeremiah laments that his mother bore him. Everyone curses him, though he has wronged no one. He found God’s words and ate them with joy. He sat alone because God’s hand was on him. He asks why his pain never ends. God tells him to return and promises to make him a bronze wall.
events.detail: In 2:13 the LORD called himself a spring of living water. In verse 18 Jeremiah turns that picture against him. He asks whether God will be like a stream that fails. It is a severe charge. God’s answer in verse 19 tells the prophet himself to “return.” Then he repeats the promise made at Jeremiah’s call (1:18–19). The complaint is corrected, and the book still keeps it.

lds.text: What must Jeremiah change when God renews his charge?

events.title: Missing celebrations and pursuing hunters
events.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah not to marry or have children in this place. Parents and children there will die and lie unburied. He must not enter a house of mourning or comfort anyone. He must not enter a house of feasting. The sounds of weddings will stop. When people ask why, he must say they have left the LORD. Yet a day will come when God brings Israel back from the north. Nations will come and admit their fathers inherited lies.
events.detail: Jeremiah receives three bans. He may not marry (verse 2), mourn (verse 5), or feast (verse 8). His own life becomes a sign of what is coming. The ordinary rites of grief and joy are about to stop for everyone. Verse 5 gives the reason for the second ban. God has withdrawn his peace, kindness, and mercy from this people. Chapter 15:17 shows how lonely this made the prophet.

events.title: Trust, hidden motives, and the Sabbath
events.summary: Judah’s sin is engraved on its heart with an iron pen. A person who trusts in human strength is like a shrub in the desert. A person who trusts the LORD is like a tree planted by water. The heart is more deceitful than anything, and the LORD searches it. Jeremiah asks God to heal him and to shame his persecutors. The LORD sends him to the city gates. The people must carry no loads on the Sabbath. If they obey, kings will keep entering those gates.

The tree stays green because its roots reach the stream. The shrub in verse 6 cannot even see good when it arrives. Verse 9 then warns that the heart can deceive its owner. A person may be wrong about where his trust lies.

events.title: A potter’s work and plots against Jeremiah
events.summary: The LORD sends Jeremiah to a potter’s house. The clay pot is spoiled on the wheel, and the potter reshapes it. God says Israel is like clay in his hand. If he warns a nation and it turns from evil, he will relent. If he promises good and a nation does evil, he will withhold it. He calls Judah to turn back. The people answer that it is hopeless and they will follow their own plans. Then they plot against Jeremiah.
events.detail: The clay in verse 4 is still wet and on the wheel. The potter can make it again. Verses 7–10 draw a lesson that works in both directions. A warning can be withdrawn, and so can a promise. Verse 8 gives the first case: a nation turns, and God relents. The people reply in verse 12 that nothing can change. They use hopelessness as a reason to go on as before.

events.title: A broken jar before the elders
events.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah to buy a clay jar. He must take elders and senior priests to the valley of Hinnom. There he says the people have filled the place with innocent blood. They have burned their sons as offerings to Baal. The valley will be called the Valley of Slaughter. Jeremiah breaks the jar in front of them. God will break the city like a jar that cannot be mended. Jeremiah repeats the message in the temple court.

Verse 11 says a broken jar “can’t be made whole again.” The time for reshaping can pass. Jeremiah acts this out before the nation’s leaders. He does it in the valley where children were burned (verse 5). The place and the audience are part of the message.

events.title: Pashhur attacks Jeremiah
events.summary: Pashhur, a chief officer of the temple, hears Jeremiah’s words. He has Jeremiah beaten and locked in the stocks. The next day Jeremiah gives him a new name: Terror on Every Side. Then Jeremiah complains to the LORD. He says God overpowered him, and he has become a joke. If he tries to keep silent, the word burns like fire in his bones. He praises the LORD as a mighty warrior. Then he curses the day he was born.
events.detail: Jeremiah is caught between two pains. When he speaks, people mock him (verse 8). When he holds back, verse 9 says a fire burns in his bones. He cannot keep it in. Verses 11–13 then speak with trust and praise. Verses 14–18 curse his birth, as Job did. The book places both in one voice and does not explain the change.

events.title: Zedekiah asks for rescue
events.summary: King Zedekiah sends two officials to Jeremiah. Babylon’s king is attacking, and they hope the LORD will work a wonder. Jeremiah answers that God himself will fight against the city. Its people will die of sword, famine, and disease. The king will be handed to Babylon. The people may choose life by surrendering. The royal house is told to give justice every morning. It must rescue the robbed from the oppressor.
events.detail: Zedekiah hopes for a rescue like the one in Hezekiah’s day (verse 2). Verse 5 says God’s outstretched hand is now against the city. Verse 12 then speaks to the royal house about its neglected work. A king held court in the morning. He was to rescue the person robbed by a stronger one. The king asks for a wonder and is told to do justice. The city’s safety is tied to the safety of its weakest people.

events.title: Kings judged by their treatment of others
events.summary: The LORD sends Jeremiah to the king’s house. The king must do justice and protect the foreigner, orphan, and widow. If not, the palace will become a ruin. One king has been carried off and will never return. Jehoiakim builds a grand house with unpaid labor. His father Josiah did justice and defended the poor. Jehoiakim will have a donkey’s burial. The young king Coniah will be thrown out like a broken pot.

Verse 15 asks whether cedar panels make a man a king. It then points to his father Josiah. Josiah ate and drank well and still did justice. Verse 16 says he judged the cause of the poor and needy. It adds, “Wasn’t this to know me?”

events.title: Harmful leaders and prophets who promise peace
events.summary: The LORD condemns the shepherds who scatter his flock. He will gather the remnant and raise a righteous Branch for David. That king will be called “The LORD our righteousness.” Jeremiah’s heart is broken because of the prophets. They commit adultery, live in lies, and encourage evildoers. They speak visions from their own minds. They tell those who despise God that all will be well. God says his word is like fire and like a hammer.
events.detail: The false prophets claim to know God’s mind. Verse 18 asks who has really stood in his council. Verse 22 gives a test that anyone can apply. A prophet who had stood there would turn people from evil. These prophets do the opposite. Verse 14 says they strengthen the hands of evildoers. Verse 17 says they promise peace to people who despise the LORD.

events.title: Two baskets of figs
events.summary: Babylon has carried off King Jeconiah, the officials, and the craftsmen. The LORD shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs before the temple. One holds very good figs, and the other holds figs too bad to eat. The good figs are the exiles in Babylon. God will watch over them and bring them back. He will give them a heart to know him. The bad figs are King Zedekiah and those left in the land. They will become a horror to all kingdoms.
events.detail: Those left in Jerusalem thought they were the favored ones (Ezekiel 11:15). The exiles looked like people God had thrown away. Verse 5 reverses that judgment. The exiles are the good figs. Verse 6 turns the hard verbs of 1:10 into promises. God will build and plant them. Verse 7 adds a gift they could not make: a heart to know him.

events.title: Babylon’s rule and the cup of anger
events.summary: In Jehoiakim’s fourth year Jeremiah speaks to all Judah. For twenty-three years he has warned them, and they have not listened. So the LORD will bring Nebuchadnezzar, his servant, against the land. The nations will serve Babylon’s king for seventy years. Then God will punish Babylon for its own guilt. Jeremiah takes a cup of wrath to the nations. Jerusalem drinks first, and Babylon’s king drinks last. The LORD will roar from on high against all the earth.
events.detail: Verse 9 calls Babylon’s king “my servant.” Verse 12 says God will punish that king and nation. Being used by God is not the same as being approved. Babylon answers for its own wrongs. The seventy years set a limit of about a lifetime. The exile will be neither short nor endless. The cup in verses 18–26 starts with Jerusalem and ends with Babylon.
