events.title: Jeremiah faces a death charge
events.summary: Early in Jehoiakim’s reign Jeremiah speaks in the temple court. He says the house will become like Shiloh unless the people change. Priests and prophets seize him and demand his death. Officials come and hold a hearing at the gate. Jeremiah says the LORD sent him and that he is in their hands. Some elders recall the prophet Micah. King Hezekiah did not kill Micah for a similar message. Another prophet, Uriah, was killed, but an official protects Jeremiah.
events.detail: The elders quote Micah 3:12 from about a century earlier (verse 18). Prophecies were remembered and could be cited in court. Verse 19 draws the precedent. Hezekiah feared the LORD, prayed, and the disaster did not come. So a warning of ruin is an invitation to change. Verses 20–23 add a second case with the opposite end. Uriah was killed, and one official saved Jeremiah (verse 24).

events.title: A yoke warns against rebellion
events.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah to make a yoke and wear it on his neck. He sends word to the kings of Edom, Moab, Ammon, Tyre, and Sidon. Their envoys are visiting King Zedekiah in Jerusalem. God made the earth and gives it to whom he chooses. He has given these lands to Nebuchadnezzar for a time. Any nation that will not serve Babylon will be destroyed. Jeremiah tells Zedekiah to accept the yoke and live. He warns the priests that the temple vessels will not soon return.
events.detail: Foreign envoys have gathered in Jerusalem (verse 3). They seem to be planning a revolt against Babylon. Jeremiah walks among them wearing a wooden yoke. Verse 12 gives the king his advice: serve Babylon and live. It sounds like disloyalty to his own country. His ground is in verses 5–6: the Creator has assigned this rule. Verse 7 adds that Babylon’s own time will also end.

events.title: Hananiah breaks the yoke
events.summary: In the same year the prophet Hananiah speaks in the temple. He says the LORD has broken Babylon’s yoke. Within two years the vessels and the exiled king will return. Jeremiah answers that he wishes it were so. Yet he says a prophet of peace is proved only when his word comes true. Hananiah takes the yoke from Jeremiah’s neck and breaks it. Jeremiah goes away. Later he tells Hananiah that he will die that year, and he does.
events.detail: Both prophets speak in the LORD’s name in the same place. Jeremiah first wishes that Hananiah were right (verse 6). Verse 9 then gives the test. Earlier prophets warned of war, so a promise of peace must be proved. Time will show who was sent. Hananiah breaks the yoke, and Jeremiah simply leaves (verses 10–11). A dramatic act does not settle the dispute.

events.title: A letter to people in exile
events.summary: Jeremiah sends a letter from Jerusalem to the exiles in Babylon. The LORD tells them to build houses and plant gardens. They should marry and have children. They should seek the peace of the city and pray for it. Prophets who promise a quick return are lying. After seventy years God will bring them back. He has plans for their peace and a future with hope. Jeremiah also answers a man who wrote from Babylon against him.
events.detail: The letter names homes, gardens, marriages, and the city’s peace. Verse 7 asks the exiles to pray for Babylon, their captor. Their own welfare is bound up with that city’s welfare. Verse 5 uses “build” and “plant” from 1:10 for a foreign land. An Egyptian scribe’s palette shows the tools behind such a letter. The promise of verse 11 comes with a date of seventy years. Most who heard it would live out their lives in exile.

events.title: Healing after national suffering
events.summary: The LORD tells Jeremiah to write his words in a book. Days are coming when he will restore Israel and Judah. There is a cry of terror, and it is a time of trouble for Jacob. Yet Jacob will be saved out of it. God will break the yoke from their necks. Their wound seems beyond cure, and their allies have forgotten them. God will restore their health and heal their wounds. The city will be rebuilt, and songs of thanks will rise from it.
events.detail: Verse 12 calls the wound incurable. Verse 14 says God himself struck the blow. Verse 17 then says the same God will heal it. The verse gives a reason drawn from an insult. Others called Zion an outcast that no one cares for. God answers the injury and the shame together. The one whom nobody seeks is sought by him.

events.title: Return and a law written in hearts
events.summary: The LORD says he has loved Israel with an everlasting love. He will rebuild her, and she will dance again. He will gather the scattered from the north, with the blind and the lame. Rachel weeps for her children, and God tells her there is hope. He will watch over his people to build and to plant. He will make a new covenant with Israel and Judah. He will write his law on their hearts. He will forgive their wrongs and remember their sin no more.
events.detail: The first covenant was written on stone tablets (Exodus 31:18). Chapter 17:1 said Judah’s sin was engraved on its heart. Verse 33 puts God’s law in that same place. Verse 32 says the people broke the earlier covenant. The new one changes where the law lives. Verse 34 rests it all on forgiveness. Hebrews 8:8–12 quotes this passage in full.

events.title: Jeremiah buys a field during the siege
events.summary: Jerusalem is under siege, and Jeremiah is held in the court of the guard. His cousin comes and asks him to buy a field in Anathoth. Jeremiah weighs out seventeen shekels of silver. He signs and seals the deed before witnesses. He gives the deeds to Baruch to store in a clay jar. The LORD says houses and fields will again be bought in this land. Jeremiah prays and asks why he should buy land the enemy holds. God answers that nothing is too hard for him.
events.detail: The field lies in territory the enemy already controls. On any market it is worthless. Jeremiah still follows every legal step (verses 10–12). Verse 14 orders the deeds kept in a jar “that they may last many days.” The wait will be long. The purchase puts money behind the promise in verse 15. The tablet offers an earlier regional comparison for recording land sales.

events.title: Healing, a just ruler, and renewed worship
events.summary: The LORD speaks to Jeremiah a second time in the court of the guard. Houses have been torn down for defense and filled with the dead. God will bring health and healing to the city. He will cleanse and forgive the people. The sounds of joy will be heard again in the empty streets. Shepherds will again count their flocks. God will raise a righteous Branch for David. His covenant with David is as sure as day and night.
events.detail: Three times Jeremiah said the bridegroom and bride would fall silent (7:34; 16:9). Verse 11 brings those very sounds back. Restoration is described in ordinary terms. People hold weddings and sing thanks in the LORD’s house. The song they sing is the refrain of Psalm 136. Verse 13 adds shepherds counting sheep. A healed land is one where daily life goes on.

events.title: Freed servants are forced back into slavery
events.summary: Babylon’s army is attacking Jerusalem and the last towns of Judah. Jeremiah tells King Zedekiah the city will fall. Zedekiah and the people make a covenant to free their Hebrew slaves. They release them and then force them back. The LORD recalls his law that slaves go free in the seventh year. The people did right for a moment and then profaned his name. So God proclaims a “liberty” for them to sword, disease, and famine. The Babylonian army will return and burn the city.
events.detail: Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12 required freedom after six years of service. The owners freed their slaves while the siege pressed them (verses 8–10). Verse 21 shows the army had pulled back for a time. Verse 16 says the owners then took the people back. They had sworn the release in the temple, so they profaned God’s name. A promise made under fear was dropped when the fear eased. Verse 17 turns their word “liberty” against them.

events.title: The Rechabites refuse wine
events.summary: In Jehoiakim’s days the LORD sends Jeremiah to the Rechabite family. Jeremiah brings them into a temple room and offers them wine. They refuse, since their ancestor Jonadab forbade it. He also told them to live in tents and plant no vineyards. They have obeyed in everything. The LORD asks Judah why it will not learn from this. A family obeys a dead ancestor, and Judah ignores its God. He promises that Jonadab’s family will always have someone to serve him.
events.detail: Jonadab lived in the time of King Jehu, long before (2 Kings 10:15). His family still keeps his rules. Verse 14 sets that beside Judah’s record. God has spoken again and again, and Judah has not listened. The argument goes from the lesser to the greater. The LORD does not tell Judah to give up wine or houses. He praises the Rechabites’ loyalty, not their particular rules.

events.title: Jehoiakim burns the scroll
events.summary: In Jehoiakim’s fourth year the LORD tells Jeremiah to write his words on a scroll. Baruch writes as Jeremiah speaks. Baruch reads the scroll in the temple on a fast day. Officials hear it, are afraid, and tell Baruch and Jeremiah to hide. The scroll is read to the king beside a winter fire. He cuts off each part as it is read and burns it. He orders their arrest, but the LORD hides them. Jeremiah dictates the scroll again, with many words added.
events.detail: The scroll moves through writing, public reading, court officials, and the king. Baruch writes it with ink (verse 18); a scribe’s palette held such ink. The officials tremble when they hear it (verse 16). The king cuts and burns it column by column (verse 23). Verse 24 notes that he did not tear his clothes. His father Josiah did tear his at a reading (2 Kings 22:11). Verse 32 says the second scroll was longer than the first.

events.title: A false charge sends Jeremiah to prison
events.summary: Zedekiah is king, and no one listens to Jeremiah. The king asks him to pray for the city. Egypt’s army marches out, and the Babylonians withdraw from Jerusalem. Jeremiah says they will return and burn the city. He tries to leave for his family land in Benjamin. A guard arrests him as a deserter. He is beaten and kept in a dungeon for many days. The king questions him in secret and moves him to the court of the guard.
events.detail: The siege has lifted, and hope rises in the city. Verse 9 warns the people not to deceive themselves. The Babylonians “will not depart.” Verse 10 makes the point in an extreme form. Even an army of wounded men would rise and burn the city. A short change in the war proves nothing. Jeremiah’s advice to surrender also makes the desertion charge easy to believe (verse 13).

events.title: Ebedmelech rescues Jeremiah
events.summary: Officials hear Jeremiah say that those who surrender will live. They tell the king he is weakening the soldiers. The king says he cannot stop them. They lower Jeremiah into a cistern, and he sinks in the mud. Ebedmelech, an Ethiopian servant of the palace, tells the king. With thirty men he pulls Jeremiah out with ropes padded by old rags. The king meets Jeremiah in secret and is urged to surrender. He is too afraid to do it.

Ebedmelech speaks to the king in public at the gate (verses 7–9). Verse 11 records where he found old rags and worn clothes. Verse 12 says they were to pad the ropes under Jeremiah’s arms. He thinks of a starved man’s skin. Chapter 39:15–18 gives him the LORD’s promise of safety.

events.title: Jerusalem falls and Jeremiah is spared
events.summary: After a siege of a year and a half the wall of Jerusalem is breached. Babylon’s officers sit in the Middle Gate. Zedekiah flees at night and is caught near Jericho. His sons are killed in front of him, and he is blinded. The city is burned, and its walls are broken down. Most of the people are taken to Babylon. The poorest are left behind and given vineyards and fields. Jeremiah is released, and Ebedmelech receives a promise of life.

The Ethiopian is promised his life (verses 16–18). Verse 10 says the poor, who owned nothing, received land. The text reports this and gives no motive for it. Jeremiah had charged the rich with seizing others’ goods (5:27–28; 22:13).

events.title: Gedaliah governs the remaining people
events.summary: The captain of the guard frees Jeremiah and lets him choose where to live. Jeremiah goes to Gedaliah, the governor Babylon appointed at Mizpah. Judah’s scattered army officers come to Gedaliah. He tells them to serve Babylon and it will go well. They should gather wine, summer fruit, and oil. Jews return from Moab, Ammon, and Edom and bring in a large harvest. An officer warns Gedaliah that a man named Ishmael plans to kill him. Gedaliah does not believe it.
events.detail: Gedaliah’s plan in verse 10 is simple. He will deal with the Babylonians, and the people will farm. They should gather the harvest and live in their towns. Verses 11–12 show it working, as refugees return to a good crop. The recovery depends on one man. Verse 16 shows him refusing to believe a warning. In verses 2–3 a Babylonian officer states Jeremiah’s own message.

events.title: Ishmael kills Gedaliah and takes captives
events.summary: Ishmael, a man of the royal family, comes to Mizpah with ten men. They eat with Gedaliah and then kill him and those with him. The next day Ishmael murders seventy pilgrims on their way to the temple. He throws the bodies into a cistern. He takes the people of Mizpah captive and heads for Ammon. Johanan and the other officers catch him at Gibeon. The captives are freed, and Ishmael escapes. The survivors camp near Bethlehem, ready to go to Egypt.
events.detail: The murder happens at a shared meal (verses 1–2). One killing ends the recovery described in chapter 40. Verse 18 gives the survivors’ reasoning. Babylon appointed Gedaliah, and Babylon will blame everyone for his death. Fear now drives their choices. Verse 5 shows pilgrims from the north still bringing offerings to a ruined temple. They are among the dead.

events.title: Survivors ask for guidance
events.summary: The officers and all the people come to Jeremiah. They ask him to pray that the LORD will show them the way. They promise to obey, whether the answer is pleasant or not. After ten days the word comes. If they stay in the land, God will build them up and plant them. They need not fear the king of Babylon. If they go to Egypt, the sword and famine will follow them there. Jeremiah says they deceived themselves when they asked.
events.detail: Verse 6 is a promise made before the answer is known. The people will obey “whether it is good, or whether it is bad.” They had already camped on the road to Egypt (41:17). Verse 7 makes them wait ten days. The answer goes against the plan they had formed. Verse 10 offers the building and planting of 1:10. Verse 20 says they misled themselves when they asked.

events.title: The survivors reject the answer
events.summary: The officers tell Jeremiah he is lying. They say Baruch has turned him against them. They lead all the people into Egypt, with Jeremiah and Baruch. They settle at Tahpanhes. There the LORD tells Jeremiah to bury large stones at the entrance to Pharaoh’s house. Nebuchadnezzar will set his throne over those stones. He will strike Egypt and burn the houses of its gods.
events.detail: The people promised to obey any answer (42:6). In verse 2 they call the answer a lie. Verse 3 gives their way out. They do not address the warning itself. They accuse the scribe Baruch of hidden motives. Blaming a third person lets them reject the message. Jeremiah is taken to the very place he warned against, and he keeps speaking there.

events.title: A dispute about the queen of the sky
events.summary: The LORD’s word comes to the Jews living across Egypt. They have seen Jerusalem ruined because of offerings to other gods. Jeremiah asks why they repeat that sin in Egypt. The men and women answer that they will not listen. They will keep burning incense to the queen of the sky. When they did so in Judah, they had food and safety. Since they stopped, they have lacked everything. Jeremiah answers that the LORD remembered those offerings, and events will show whose word stands.
events.detail: Both sides argue from the same events. The people say trouble began when they stopped their offerings (verse 18). Jeremiah says trouble came because they made them (verses 21–23). Each reads the past as proof. Verse 17 shows the people appealing to their fathers and kings. The dispute is about the remembered cause of a disaster. Verse 28 leaves the test to the outcome.

events.title: Baruch receives a promise of survival
events.summary: This short word is for Baruch, Jeremiah’s scribe. It dates from the year he wrote the scroll. Baruch has said that the LORD added sorrow to his pain. He is worn out and finds no rest. The LORD says he is tearing down what he built across the whole land. He asks whether Baruch seeks great things for himself. Baruch should not seek them. He will keep his life wherever he goes.
events.detail: Baruch came from a family of officials; his brother served the king (51:59). He could have hoped for a career. Verse 4 puts God’s own loss first. God is breaking down what he himself built and planted. Against that, verse 5 asks about Baruch’s private hopes. Personal ambition is out of scale in such a time. He is promised one thing: his life.

events.title: Egypt’s armies face defeat
events.summary: This is the first of Jeremiah’s messages about foreign nations. Egypt’s army is defeated at Carchemish by the king of Babylon. Its soldiers are terrified and fall back. Egypt rose like the Nile and said it would cover the earth. No medicine will heal it. A second message says Nebuchadnezzar will invade Egypt itself. Pharaoh is called a loud noise who missed his moment. Afterward Egypt will be lived in again, and Jacob need not fear.
events.detail: The Nile’s yearly flood was Egypt’s strength and pride. Verse 8 uses it as a picture of the army. Egypt says it will rise and cover the earth. Verses 5–6 have already shown the soldiers running. The boast and the outcome stand side by side. Verse 17 gives Pharaoh a mocking nickname. Verse 26 still says Egypt will be inhabited again.
events.uncertainty: Lines join the places Jeremiah names, in order. They do not trace real roads or sea lanes.

lds.text: How does Egypt’s boast differ from the soldiers’ flight?

events.title: A warning against the Philistines
events.summary: This message concerns the Philistines. Waters rise from the north and become an overflowing flood. People cry out at the sound of horses and chariots. Fathers are too weak to turn back for their children. Tyre and Sidon lose their last helpers. Gaza and Ashkelon are silenced. A voice asks how long the LORD’s sword will keep striking. The answer is that the LORD has given it an order.
events.detail: Verse 6 speaks to the sword itself. A voice asks how long before it will be quiet. It begs the sword to go back into its sheath. Verse 7 answers that it cannot rest while it has orders. The message is against an old enemy of Israel. It still contains a cry for the killing to stop. Verse 3 shows the cost: fathers who cannot help their children.

lds.text: Why does the passage ask the sword to rest?

events.title: Moab’s pride and suffering
events.summary: This long message concerns Moab. Its towns are named one by one as they fall. Its god Chemosh goes into exile with his priests. Moab has been at ease since its youth, like wine left undisturbed. It mocked Israel and was very proud. The speaker wails for Moab and weeps for its vineyards. Joy and gladness are gone from its fields. Yet the LORD will restore Moab’s fortunes in the last days.
events.detail: Verse 29 states the charge against Moab: great pride. Verse 27 adds that it laughed at Israel. Then verse 31 says, “I will wail for Moab.” The voice that judges also mourns. Verse 36 says the speaker’s heart moans like a flute. Judgment and grief come from the same mouth. Verse 47 ends the chapter with a promise of restoration.

events.title: Warnings against neighboring peoples
events.summary: This chapter gathers messages about five peoples. Ammon trusted in its treasures and will see its capital ruined. Edom trusted in its wisdom and its high cliffs. Damascus grows weak, and its young men fall in the streets. The desert tribes of Kedar lose their tents and camels. Elam’s bow is broken, and its people are scattered. Ammon and Elam are promised restoration afterward. God says he will keep Edom’s orphans alive.
events.detail: Each people in this chapter relied on something different. Ammon had treasure and fertile valleys (verse 4). Edom had wisdom and cliffs (verses 7 and 16). Damascus had fame, Kedar had distance, and Elam had the bow. Every one of these protections fails. The endings are not the same. Ammon and Elam are restored, and Edom’s orphans are kept (verses 6, 11, 39).

events.title: Babylon faces judgment
events.summary: This message announces the fall of Babylon. Its gods are put to shame, and a nation from the north attacks. Israel and Judah come weeping and ask the way to Zion. They have been lost sheep, misled by their shepherds. Their enemies said harming them was no crime, since they had sinned. Assyria devoured Israel, and Babylon gnawed its bones. God will punish Babylon as he punished Assyria. The hammer of the whole earth is broken.
events.detail: Verse 7 quotes the enemies’ defense. Israel sinned against the LORD, so those who devoured it are “not guilty.” They borrow the prophets’ own teaching to excuse themselves. The chapter rejects that excuse. Verse 11 says Babylon rejoiced as it plundered. Verse 29 says it was proud against the LORD. Being the means of judgment did not make its cruelty innocent.

lds.text: Why does Babylon remain responsible after serving as an instrument of judgment?

events.title: A scroll marks Babylon’s announced fall
events.summary: The LORD will send a destroying wind against Babylon. Babylon was a golden cup that made the whole earth drunk. Now it falls suddenly, and its wound cannot be healed. The LORD made the earth by his power, and idols are nothing. Zion says Nebuchadnezzar swallowed her like a monster. Babylon’s thick walls will be leveled. Jeremiah writes all this in a scroll and gives it to an officer named Seraiah. Seraiah must read it in Babylon and sink it in the Euphrates.
events.detail: Verse 59 dates this to Zedekiah’s fourth year. In that same period Jeremiah told the exiles to pray for Babylon (29:7). The exiles should seek the city’s peace, and its fall is already written. Jeremiah wrote this in a book (verse 60); the palette shows a scribe’s tools. Seraiah is to read the scroll aloud in Babylon. A stone then sends the scroll beneath the river’s surface. Verse 64 explains the act: Babylon will sink and not rise.

lds.text: Why does Jeremiah tell Seraiah to sink the scroll after reading it?

events.title: Jerusalem’s destruction and Jehoiachin’s release
events.summary: This last chapter retells the fall of Jerusalem. Zedekiah rebels, and Babylon besieges the city until the food is gone. The wall is breached, and the king is caught and blinded. The temple, the palace, and the houses are burned. The bronze pillars and vessels of the temple are carried away. The chief priests and officials are executed. The numbers of the exiles are listed. Years later the king of Babylon frees Jehoiachin and feeds him at his table.
events.detail: Chapter 51:64 said Jeremiah’s words ended there. This chapter adds history that matches 2 Kings 25. It shows that the city fell as he had said. Verses 17–23 list the temple’s bronze piece by piece as it is taken. Nothing is said to repair that loss. Verse 31 then reports a small mercy to a captive king. The book ends with a ruined temple and a living heir of David.

ancientRoads.title: International coastal highway
ancientRoads.summary: This major route linked Egypt with the coast and northern Levant. Traders, messengers, and imperial armies used its plains and passes.
ancientRoads.detail: The southern section followed the coast through Gaza and Philistia. Farther north, important branches crossed Carmel and the Jezreel Valley. “Via Maris” is a familiar later name. This guide calls it the international coastal highway.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: Strong evidence supports this route. The line shows a general path. Its branches and exact roadbeds changed over time.

ancientRoads.title: Jezreel Valley–Damascus route
ancientRoads.summary: This branch connected Megiddo and the Jezreel Valley with Beth Shean. It continued toward the upper Jordan region and Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: The valley and its crossings supported trade and army travel. The route joined the coast, Galilee, Transjordan, and inland Syria.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The main connection is well supported. The line shows a broad route, not one fixed or fully built road.

ancientRoads.title: Central ridge road
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south road followed the central hills. It passed Beersheba, Hebron, Jerusalem, Bethel, and Shechem. It continued toward the Jezreel Valley.
ancientRoads.detail: This route linked the principal highland settlements of Judah and Israel. It avoided some lowland obstacles but still depended on ridges, saddles, and local descents.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The hill route is well supported. The exact track could divide or shift between nearby ridges and towns.

ancientRoads.title: Jordan Valley and Arabah route
ancientRoads.summary: A long north–south route used the Arabah and Jordan Valley. It joined Aqaba, the Dead Sea, Jericho, Beth Shean, and Galilee.
ancientRoads.detail: Travelers used several tracks on both sides of the valley. Fords and seasonal conditions affected where people crossed the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The valley route is well supported. The line combines several possible tracks. It does not mark specific river crossings.

ancientRoads.title: Shephelah road
ancientRoads.summary: This route ran through Judah’s western lowlands. It joined Beersheba, Lachish, Gezer, Aphek, and the valleys below Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.detail: The Shephelah formed a connected lowland zone between the coastal plain and the Judean hills. Fortified towns near the route guarded approaches into the highlands.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional route is well supported. Local branches between valleys and fortified towns are simplified.

ancientRoads.title: Beth-horon ascent
ancientRoads.summary: This important western route connected the coastal plain with Jerusalem. It passed through the Aijalon Valley and climbed Beth-horon.
ancientRoads.detail: The ascent used a favorable pass through difficult hill country. It served traffic between the coast, the Benjamin plateau, and Jerusalem.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The pass and connection are well supported. The line does not claim an exact roadbed at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Lachish–Jerusalem approaches
ancientRoads.summary: Routes through the Shephelah valleys connected Lachish with Jerusalem. They also joined nearby walled towns with the Judean hills.
ancientRoads.detail: Second Kings 18:17 sends an Assyrian army from Lachish up to Jerusalem. The text does not name the road. This line shows one common approach.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is probable. The exact track is unknown, so the line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Jerusalem–Jericho road
ancientRoads.summary: This steep east–west route connected Jerusalem with Jericho and the Jordan Valley. It also reached crossings toward Transjordan.
ancientRoads.detail: The road descended rapidly through dry and broken terrain. It gave Jerusalem access to the valley and to routes east of the Jordan.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection is well supported. The displayed bends are approximate and do not identify one preserved Iron Age roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Transjordan plateau route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route crossed the Transjordan plateau. It passed Edom, Moab, Ammon, and Gilead before reaching Damascus.
ancientRoads.detail: This series of plateau roads is often called the King’s Highway. It supported trade east of the Jordan. It linked nearby towns with Arabia, Syria, and western crossings.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: This broad route is well known. It was not one fully built road. Its path and local branches remain uncertain.

ancientRoads.title: Damascus–Hamath–Aleppo route
ancientRoads.summary: A north–south inland route connected Damascus with the Orontes valley, Hamath, and Aleppo.
ancientRoads.detail: Aleppo stood where many major routes met. They linked Anatolia, Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Mediterranean. This line follows the broad route through the Orontes valley, not the desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is well supported. The evidence does not show one fixed Iron Age track. The line is dashed.

ancientRoads.title: Aleppo–Euphrates approach
ancientRoads.summary: This road linked Aleppo with the Euphrates crossing near Til Barsip. Assyria’s state road began there.
ancientRoads.detail: Assyrian records and studies of ancient land support this route. It went through the Sajur and Manbij area. It then crossed the Jabbul plain toward Aleppo.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The connection and principal approach are well supported. The displayed bends simplify several local valleys and possible parallel tracks.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian King’s Road to Nineveh
ancientRoads.summary: The Neo-Assyrian state road connected western lands with the Assyrian heartland. It ended at the capital city of Nineveh.
ancientRoads.detail: The route crossed the Euphrates at Til Barsip. It crossed the Balih south of Harran. It also crossed Habur streams between Guzana and Nasibina. It then reached the Tigris at Nineveh. Royal messengers changed mules at road stations.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The named crossings and stations are well supported. The line between them is a broad regional path, not a surveyed roadbed.

ancientRoads.title: Assyrian Tigris route
ancientRoads.summary: A major north–south route followed the Tigris. It linked Nineveh, Kalhu, and Assur in the Assyrian heartland.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu held a central position between Assur and Nineveh. It supported long trips by land and river. Kalhu later became an Assyrian royal capital.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The cities and their connection are well supported. The line shows a broad route. It does not separate land travel from river travel at every point.

ancientRoads.title: Arbela–Babylonia route
ancientRoads.summary: An eastern branch connected Kalhu with Arbela. It followed the western edge of the Zagros Mountains. Other routes continued south into Babylonia.
ancientRoads.detail: Kalhu controlled an eastward route through Arbela. The route followed the western edge of the Zagros toward Babylonia. It avoided a direct crossing of the central desert.
ancientRoads.uncertainty: The regional connection is supported, but the precise southern alignment and stations are uncertain. The line is dashed.

regions.detail: Ammon’s king sends Ishmael to kill Gedaliah (Jeremiah 40:14). Ezekiel 25 speaks against Ammon.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide to the land around Rabbah.

regions.name: Moab · approximate
regions.summary: Moab was a kingdom on the high land east of the Dead Sea. Dibon was its capital.
regions.detail: Jeremiah 48 speaks against Moab. Moabite raiders attack Judah in 2 Kings 24:2.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Numbers 21:26 says Moab once lost land north of the Arnon.

regions.name: Edom · approximate
regions.summary: Edom was a kingdom south of the Dead Sea. The Bible calls its people the children of Esau.
regions.detail: Obadiah and Lamentations 4 speak against Edom. Obadiah says Edom stood aside when strangers took Jerusalem.
regions.uncertainty: The shape is a simple guide. Edom’s people later moved west into southern Judah.

guides.title: Jeremiah: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: A temple can become a false source of safety
steps.text: Verse 4 quotes a phrase the people repeat three times. They treat the building as a guarantee. Verse 9 lists what they do during the week. It names theft, murder, adultery, false oaths, and other gods. Verse 11 calls the temple a robbers’ den, a hideout where thieves feel safe. Verse 12 points to Shiloh, an earlier holy place that fell (1 Samuel 4). Jesus quotes verse 11 in Matthew 21:13.

steps.title: A land purchase gives hope a material form
steps.text: The field lies in territory the enemy already controls. On any market it is worthless. Jeremiah still follows every legal step (verses 10–12). Verse 14 orders the deeds kept in a jar “that they may last many days.” The wait will be long. The purchase puts money behind the promise in verse 15. The tablet offers an earlier regional comparison for recording land sales.

steps.title: Destroying a copy does not end the message
steps.text: The scroll moves through writing, public reading, court officials, and the king. Baruch writes it with ink (verse 18); a scribe’s palette held such ink. The officials tremble when they hear it (verse 16). The king cuts and burns it column by column (verse 23). Verse 24 notes that he did not tear his clothes. His father Josiah did tear his at a reading (2 Kings 22:11). Verse 32 says the second scroll was longer than the first.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jeremiah is a priest’s son from the village of Anathoth. The LORD’s word comes to him in the days of King Josiah. God says he knew Jeremiah before he was formed in the womb. He has appointed him a prophet to the nations. Jeremiah answers that he is only a youth and cannot speak. The LORD touches his mouth and puts words in it. Jeremiah sees an almond branch and a boiling pot tilted from the north. God promises to make him like a fortified city against the whole land.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD remembers Israel’s early devotion, like a bride who followed him in the desert. He asks what fault their fathers found in him. Priests, rulers, and prophets all turned away. No other nation has traded its gods, yet Israel traded its glory. The people left the spring of living water. They dug cracked tanks that hold no water. They run to Egypt and Assyria for help. They say to a tree, “You are my father.”

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD compares Judah to an unfaithful wife who still expects to return. In Josiah’s days he points to the northern kingdom. Israel was unfaithful and was sent away. Her sister Judah saw it and was not afraid. Judah returned to God only in pretense. So God calls Israel less guilty than Judah. He invites the north to return and only admit its guilt. He promises shepherds after his own heart and healing for the faithless.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD says Israel may return if she puts away her idols. Judah must break up its unplowed ground. A trumpet warns of disaster from the north. A lion has left its thicket to ruin the land. Jeremiah cries out in anguish at the sound of war. He sees the earth empty and the heavens without light. Mountains shake, people are gone, and the birds have fled. Yet the LORD says he will not make a full end.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells Jeremiah to search Jerusalem for one person who does justice. If he finds one, God will pardon the city. Jeremiah thinks the poor simply do not know God’s way. He goes to the great men, and they too have broken free. A distant nation will come and devour their harvest. The people have eyes and do not see. Rich men grow fat and do not defend the orphan. Prophets lie, priests rule by their own authority, and the people love it.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jeremiah warns the people of Benjamin to flee Jerusalem. An army from the north prepares to attack. No one listens, for their ears are closed. Everyone is greedy, from the least to the greatest. Prophets and priests say “Peace, peace” when there is no peace. They do not know how to blush. God tells them to ask for the old paths and find rest. They answer that they will not walk in them.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jeremiah stands at the temple gate and speaks to those who enter. He tells them to change their ways. They must not trust the words “The LORD’s temple.” They must do justice and stop oppressing foreigners, orphans, and widows. They steal, murder, and worship Baal, then come and say they are safe. God asks whether his house has become a den of robbers. He tells them to remember what he did to Shiloh. They even burn their children in the valley of Hinnom.

chapterMaps.narrative: The bones of Judah’s kings and priests will be spread under the sky. The LORD asks why the people never turn back. Even the stork knows its seasons. The people say they are wise and have the LORD’s law. Yet the scribes’ pen has turned it into a lie. Leaders say “Peace” when there is no peace. Jeremiah’s heart is sick for his people. He asks whether there is no balm in Gilead.

The LORD will refine and test them. Jerusalem will become a heap of ruins. He calls for the mourning women, since death has climbed through the windows. The wise, the strong, and the rich must not boast. Let a person boast only in knowing the LORD.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells Israel not to learn the ways of the nations. A craftsman cuts a tree and decorates it with silver and gold. He fastens it with nails so that it will not fall. Such idols cannot speak or walk. No one is like the LORD, the living God. He made the earth by his power. Jeremiah mourns that his tent is destroyed. He admits that a person cannot direct his own steps.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells Jeremiah to proclaim the terms of the covenant. The fathers were told to obey when they left Egypt. They did not, and their children have returned to those sins. God tells Jeremiah not to pray for them. Then the LORD shows Jeremiah a plot against his life. He had been like a gentle lamb led to slaughter. The men of Anathoth tell him to stop prophesying or die. God says he will punish them.

chapterMaps.narrative: Jeremiah brings a case before the LORD. He asks why the wicked prosper and the faithless live at ease. He asks how long the land must mourn. God answers with a question. If running with men has tired him, how will he race horses? Even his own family has betrayed him. God says he has left his house and given his beloved to enemies. Yet he will later have compassion on the neighbors who harmed Israel.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells Jeremiah to buy a linen belt and wear it. Then he must hide it in a rock by the river. After many days he digs it up, and it is ruined. God says he will ruin Judah’s pride in the same way. As a belt clings to the waist, he made Israel cling to him. They would not listen. Jeremiah warns the king and the queen mother that their crowns will fall. He asks whether a leopard can change its spots.

chapterMaps.narrative: A drought strikes Judah. Nobles send servants for water, and the cisterns are empty. The ground is cracked, and even the deer abandons her fawn. The people admit their sins and ask God to act for his name’s sake. God tells Jeremiah not to pray for them. Jeremiah says the prophets are promising peace. The LORD answers that he did not send those prophets. They and those who believe them will fall by sword and famine.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD says he would not relent even if Moses and Samuel pleaded. The people are assigned to death, sword, famine, and exile. Jeremiah laments that his mother bore him. Everyone curses him, though he has wronged no one. He found God’s words and ate them with joy. He sat alone because God’s hand was on him. He asks why his pain never ends. God tells him to return and promises to make him a bronze wall.

chapterMaps.narrative: The LORD tells Jeremiah not to marry or have children in this place. Parents and children there will die and lie unburied. He must not enter a house of mourning or comfort anyone. He must not enter a house of feasting. The sounds of weddings will stop. When people ask why, he must say they have left the LORD. textRoutes.title: A letter to people in exile
textRoutes.summary: Jeremiah sends a letter from Jerusalem to the exiles in Babylon. The LORD tells them to build houses and plant gardens. They should marry and have children. They should seek the peace of the city and pray for it. Prophets who promise a quick return are lying. After seventy years God will bring them back. He has plans for their peace and a future with hope. Jeremiah also answers a man who wrote from Babylon against him.
textRoutes.detail: The letter names homes, gardens, marriages, and the city’s peace. Verse 7 asks the exiles to pray for Babylon, their captor. Their own welfare is bound up with that city’s welfare. Verse 5 uses “build” and “plant” from 1:10 for a foreign land. An Egyptian scribe’s palette shows the tools behind such a letter. The promise of verse 11 comes with a date of seventy years. Most who heard it would live out their lives in exile.

textRoutes.title: Jerusalem falls and Jeremiah is spared
textRoutes.summary: After a siege of a year and a half the wall of Jerusalem is breached. Babylon’s officers sit in the Middle Gate. Zedekiah flees at night and is caught near Jericho. textRoutes.detail: The chapter gives very different ends to different people. The king loses his sons and his sight (verses 6–7). The prophet is freed on Babylon’s orders (verses 11–14). The Ethiopian is promised his life (verses 16–18). Verse 10 says the poor, who owned nothing, received land. The text reports this and gives no motive for it. Jeremiah had charged the rich with seizing others’ goods (5:27–28; 22:13).

textRoutes.title: Gedaliah governs the remaining people
textRoutes.summary: The captain of the guard frees Jeremiah and lets him choose where to live. Jeremiah goes to Gedaliah, the governor Babylon appointed at Mizpah. Judah’s scattered army officers come to Gedaliah. He tells them to serve Babylon and it will go well. They should gather wine, summer fruit, and oil. Jews return from Moab, Ammon, and Edom and bring in a large harvest. An officer warns Gedaliah that a man named Ishmael plans to kill him. Gedaliah does not believe it.

Verses 11–12 show it working, as refugees return to a good crop. The recovery depends on one man. Verse 16 shows him refusing to believe a warning. In verses 2–3 a Babylonian officer states Jeremiah’s own message.
